title: Spectroscopy of low-lying valley states in hot Si/SiGe quantum dots
authors: Connor Nasseraddin, Heun Mo Yoo, Tanner M. Janda, Jason R. Petta
abstract: The presence of low-lying valley states in Si may hinder the development of large-scale spin-based quantum processors. Rapid prototyping of novel Si/SiGe heterostructures and gate stacks will be central to identifying pathways that increase the valley splitting. We compare the performance of pulsed-gate spectroscopy (PGS) and detuning axis spectroscopy (DAPS) at temperatures up to 700 mK. We find that DAPS outperforms PGS, with DAPS resolving valley splittings as small as ~86 $μ$eV, while the energy resolution of PGS is only ~210~$μ$eV. Our work demonstrates that DAPS can be used to efficiently extract valley splittings at elevated temperatures in high throughput cryostats.
summary: The research compares two spectroscopic methods, PGS and DAPS, used to measure valley state splittings in Si/SiGe quantum dots. The study demonstrates that DAPS offers significantly higher energy resolution than PGS, especially at elevated temperatures. This finding establishes DAPS as a superior technique for characterizing the critical parameters needed for building scalable spin-based quantum processors.
main_problem: Low-lying valley states in silicon quantum dots may impede the development of large-scale spin-based quantum processors, necessitating methods to increase valley splitting.
main_result: Detuning Axis Spectroscopy (DAPS) significantly outperforms Pulsed-Gate Spectroscopy (PGS), resolving valley splittings down to $\sim 86 \mu	ext{eV}$ even at elevated temperatures ($700 	ext{ mK}$).
method: The authors compare two spectroscopic techniques, PGS and DAPS, by measuring the conductance of a double quantum dot coupled to a charge sensor.
model_or_system: The experiment uses spin qubits fabricated in Si/SiGe heterostructures containing double quantum dots (DQD). The measurements probe the energy splitting between valley states within these semiconductor nanostructures.
key_observables: Valley splitting ($E_{V,R}$), measured via spectral features in the charge sensor conductance ($g$).
important_parameters: Measurement temperatures up to $700 	ext{ mK}$; resolution limits of $\sim 86 \mu	ext{eV}$ (DAPS) vs. $\sim 210 \mu	ext{eV}$ (PGS).
main_assumptions: The superior performance of DAPS is attributed to its measurement mechanism relying only on interdot charge transitions, avoiding the thermal broadening associated with coupling to a Fermi reservoir in PGS.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the device structure and energy level diagrams. Key comparisons show the temperature dependence of spectroscopic features, demonstrating that DAPS maintains high resolution at higher temperatures than PGS.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem (valley states hindering qubits), compares two measurement techniques (PGS vs. DAPS) across varying temperatures, presents quantitative results showing DAPS's superior energy resolution, and concludes by recommending DAPS for practical quantum device characterization.
why_interesting: This work provides crucial experimental benchmarks on characterizing fundamental energy splittings in solid-state qubits, directly impacting the feasibility assessment of silicon-based quantum computing architectures.

If point ii is near an anti-crossing, enhanced charge dephasing yields a mixed charge state. (b) DAPS data obtained from the right QD. g is plotted as a function of thold and ε.
